Technical Specification v2.4 Zero-Knowledge Protocol

JChatt Cryptographic Architecture & Threat Model

Document: JCHATT-WP-2026-A Classification: Public / Open Specification Lead Authors: JChatt Protocol Engineering Group Published: 2026
Executive Abstract: JChatt is an asymmetric zero-telemetry private communications system engineered to eliminate corporate metadata harvesting, centralized directory vulnerabilities, phone number identification, and physical coercion vectors. All communication payloads are encrypted client-side via AES-256-GCM before socket transmission; identity keys are derived deterministically on-device via 12-word seed phrases; and anti-coercion vaults provide mathematically plausible deniability.

1. Threat Model & Adversarial Assumptions

JChatt is engineered against three primary classes of adversaries:

  • Adversary 1: Active Network & Relay Intermediaries (ISP, Cloud Relay, State Surveillance). We assume all network traffic traversing relay nodes and Firebase RTDB transports can be intercepted, inspected, or recorded. The adversary has full visibility into packet timing and ciphertext payloads. Defense: Zero-knowledge client-side AES-256-GCM encryption with 12-byte cryptographically secure random nonces per message; TLS 1.3 socket encapsulation; zero server knowledge of encryption keys.
  • Adversary 2: Compromised or Subpoenaed Infrastructure. We assume relay servers, database hosts, or CDN edges may be seized or subpoenaed. Defense: The relay stores zero cleartext, zero phone numbers, zero address books, and zero recovery emails. The cloud database is treated purely as a blind encrypted mailbox where all records resemble pseudorandom noise.
  • Adversary 3: Physical Device Seizure & Coerced Unlock. We assume the user may face forced inspection by hostile border agents, attackers, or coercive third parties. Defense: Dual PIN architecture (Master PIN vs Duress PIN), functional 4-function Calculator disguise mode, and isolated Decoy Storage partition. Entering a Duress PIN renders a pristine dummy chat interface with zero cryptographic pointers to the primary vault.

2. Identity Key Derivation & Sovereignty

Unlike conventional messengers that bind identity to a telecommunications IMSI/SIM card or centralized SMS verification, JChatt uses a self-sovereign seed architecture:

[ User Device CSPRNG: crypto.getRandomValues() ] │ ▼ (128-bit Entropy) 12-Word Mnemonic Wordlist (BIP39 English) │ ▼ PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 (100,000 Iterations) Master Cryptographic Seed (256-bit) ├── Key Derivation: AES-256 Key Encryption Key (KEK) └── Public Identifier Hash (Sha-256 truncate -> @handle)

The 12-word seed phrase never leaves the client's volatile memory. When stored persistently in browser storage or Android Keystore, it is encrypted under the user's device Master PIN via WebCrypto AES-GCM. If the device is destroyed, the user recreates the identical cryptographic identity on any other device without contacting any server.

3. Message Cryptography: AES-256-GCM

Every message exchanged on JChatt is encrypted using the Advanced Encryption Standard in Galois/Counter Mode (AES-256-GCM), providing both confidentiality and provable message integrity.

Component Specification Cryptographic Function
Cipher Algorithm AES-256 (NIST SP 800-38D) Symmetric payload confidentiality with 256-bit key entropy.
Initialization Vector (IV) 96-bit (12-byte) CSPRNG Generated freshly per message via crypto.getRandomValues. Replay resistant.
Authentication Tag 128-bit GMAC Tag Guarantees ciphertext integrity; detects any bit-flipping or tampering.
Key Derivation (KDF) PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 100,000 rounds salt-expanded key stretching for shared chat secrets.
Transport Protocol HTTPS / WSS / TLS 1.3 Dual-layer transport encryption wrapping encrypted ciphertexts. 
// Cryptographic Payload Format Transmitted over Relay
{
  "senderId": "anon_9f81a7b",
  "recipientId": "anon_3c4d28e",
  "ciphertext": "e2f180ba7d6c...", // AES-256-GCM encrypted UTF-8 bytes
  "iv": "9a2f7c41e890b23412567890",   // Unique 12-byte IV in hex
  "tag": "4b9e28f107c8...",          // 128-bit authentication tag
  "timestamp": 1731776400000
}

4. WebRTC Peer-to-Peer Calling & DTLS-SRTP

Voice and video calls in JChatt bypass centralized audio mixing servers. Signaling is negotiated through encrypted ephemeral handshake packets, after which direct peer-to-peer media streams are established:

  • DTLS-SRTP Encryption: Audio/Video frames are encrypted using the Secure Real-time Transport Protocol (SRTP) authenticated via Datagram Transport Layer Security (DTLS). No relay server possesses the decryption keys.
  • P2P Direct Sockets: Media packets flow directly between device IP addresses whenever NAT conditions permit.
  • STUN/TURN Fallback: In symmetric NAT scenarios, an ephemeral TURN relay forwards encrypted UDP packets without decryption capabilities.

5. Anti-Coercion & Physical Plausible Deniability

Physical access is a dominant attack vector in high-risk jurisdictions. Traditional messengers with biometric unlock leak the existence of encrypted chats the moment the device is unlocked. JChatt implements two layers of physical plausible deniability:

A. 4-Function Calculator Disguise

When Calculator Disguise is enabled in Security Settings, the app launches with the label "Calculator" and an identical iOS/Android calculator layout. It performs exact floating-point arithmetic (addition, subtraction, multiplication, square roots). The encrypted messenger is revealed only when the user enters their custom stealth secret sequence followed by = or %. To any forensic or casual observer, the application is indistinguishable from a standard utility.

B. Duress PIN & Decoy Vault Partition

Users configure two distinct PIN codes:

  • Master PIN (e.g., 1337): Unlocks the authentic primary database, keys, and encrypted conversations.
  • Duress PIN (e.g., 9999): If forced to unlock under physical threat or border checkpoint detention, entering this PIN decrypts an entirely isolated Decoy Partition pre-populated with harmless benign conversations (e.g., shopping lists, cooking recipes). The primary key vault remains completely unreferenced, preventing any forensic indication that another database exists.

6. Android Background Delivery Architecture

Modern mobile operating systems aggressively terminate background network connections. To maintain timely message alerts without relying on privacy-invasive Google Cloud Messaging payload inspection, JChatt uses a dedicated isolated Android service:

[ Device Boot / App Close ] │ ▼ Android Isolated Service (:sync) ──> Battery Whitelist Request │ ▼ Persistent SSE Stream (Server-Sent Events) Firebase RTDB Realtime Node: /v2/userChats/{uid} │ ▼ Encrypted Notification Ping High-Priority Android Heads-up Alert (Local decryption or generic chime)
  • Isolated Process: The sync worker runs in an independent Linux process (:sync) unaffected by main app UI disposal.
  • Automatic Token Refresh: Session tokens are regenerated every 50 minutes using local credentials, ensuring indefinite message listening.
  • Zero Payload Notification: Cloud notification triggers do not transmit message content in cleartext; alerts display generic sovereign indicators until unlocked.

7. Open Source Auditability

True cryptographic privacy requires absolute code transparency. JChatt is committed to reproducible, auditable open source engineering:

  • Complete repository: github.com/JJcoders00/jchatt
  • Zero proprietary analytics, zero tracking SDKs, zero third-party ads.
  • Standard WebCrypto API implementation conforming to W3C cryptographic recommendations.
